title: Legal retrieval: Provision tuning beats universal rankings
desc: Shows query optimization can improve RAG selectively, while clause scores remain task-specific and insufficient for deployment assurance.

kps.k: Legal-AI performance depends on the task and retrieval design, rather than a single measure of legal competence.
kps.d: The RAG Report tests whether a system retrieves labelled contract provisions; LegalBench reports model scores on discrete legal interpretation tasks. Together, they distinguish success in locating relevant text from success in interpreting it. Their findings do not directly conflict: retrieval optimisation can improve one stage of due diligence while models still perform unevenly on downstream tasks. Neither set of supplied results establishes end-to-end legal reliability.

qs.q: We then tested the retrieval of all instances of a given Provision (as labelled in CUAD) and calculated the Recall@10 and Recall@20 over the entire collection of contracts.
qs.a: The RAG Report: Large Language Models in Legal Due Diligence · Law firms · 2024

kps.k: Provision-specific query optimisation substantially improved retrieval in the RAG Report's experiments.
kps.d: The authors indexed all 510 CUAD contracts and compared two hybrid keyword-and-vector approaches: simple question-like queries and pre-optimised provision-specific queries. Weighted Recall@10 rose from 81.31% to 97.28% across all contracts. On contracts containing at least 20 chunks, it rose from 73.15% to 95.36%, a 22.21-percentage-point gain. The longer-contract test reduced the advantage that both approaches enjoyed when ten retrieved chunks could cover an entire short agreement.

kps.k: Retrieval gains vary by provision and retrieval budget, supporting selective rather than uniform optimisation.
kps.d: In the longer-contract Recall@10 test, exclusivity gained 63.72 percentage points, while governing law gained 1.67 points. The RAG Report therefore argues that not every provision warrants the same optimisation effort. For contracts containing at least 40 chunks, retrieving twenty chunks raised weighted recall from 83.07% to 97.95%. The authors attribute the stronger baseline largely to retrieving more chunks; because this scenario changes both document length and retrieval count, it does not isolate the effect of length alone.

kps.k: Strong contract-clause benchmark scores do not generalise across legal tasks or produce a universal model ranking.
kps.d: LegalBench reports governing-law scores of 99.3, 98.3 and 98.7 for GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Claude-1, respectively, but scores of 15.4, 31.9 and 20.7 on initial matching rights periods (cor), and 9.1, 13.7 and 5.5 on unfair terms of service. Rankings also change within contract tasks: GPT-3.5 exceeds GPT-4 on renewal-termination notice and warranty duration. Among 3B models, Flan scores 93.2 on consumer_contracts_qa but 0.0 on the separate contract_qa task, where Incite scores 82.9. These contrasts support task-specific benchmarking, not a blanket inference about a model's legal capability.

kps.k: The evidence supports targeted testing, but leaves deployment reliability and causes of performance differences unresolved.
kps.d: The RAG Report uses 3,500-character text chunks and fixed retrieval counts; it anticipates, rather than demonstrates, that tables, charts and images need different chunking or OCR. LegalBench's supplied table fragments omit the scoring definition and full testing conditions. Its tasks differ substantially in sample count and input length, but the excerpts do not establish that these differences cause score variation. A practical implication is to test retrieval and interpretation separately on the intended provisions, document lengths and formats. These results do not measure hallucination rates, human verification requirements or readiness for unsupervised legal work.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the proposition’s core claim that legal-AI performance is task-specific and cannot be captured by a universal model ranking. LegalBench reports sharp within-model variation between legal interpretation tasks and changes in which model leads: strong performance on many CUAD clause tasks coexists with weak results on some MAUD tasks, while Flan’s strong consumer-contract and contract-inference scores do not carry over to contract_qa. This is supporting rather than extending evidence because LegalBench does not test provision-specific retrieval tuning, explain the causes of score differences, or establish end-to-end deployment reliability. The material variation is therefore across benchmark tasks and models, not disagreement within the source’s overall direction.

The traditional-law-firm source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal retrieval performance is task- and design-specific, and that provision-specific optimisation can outperform a uniform retrieval approach without establishing general legal competence or deployment reliability. Its CUAD experiments report substantial recall improvements from pre-optimised provision queries, especially for longer contracts. The source also supplies the cluster’s principal qualification: gains vary markedly by provision, so optimisation should be selective rather than universal. Material internal variation concerns provision type, document length and retrieval budget; retrieving more chunks improves the baseline, while some provisions benefit far more from optimisation than others. The study is limited to retrieval of labelled text chunks—not downstream interpretation, end-to-end due diligence, non-text formats, hallucination rates or unsupervised reliability. Because this professional-voice category contains one curated source here, its position should not be generalised to traditional law firms as a whole.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that legal-AI performance is task- and design-specific, not reducible to a universal model ranking or a single claim of legal competence. The RAG Report provides direct experimental evidence that provision-specific query optimisation can materially improve retrieval recall, while also showing that gains differ sharply by provision and retrieval budget. LegalBench independently supports the broader task-specificity claim: model scores and leaders vary substantially across contract and other legal interpretation tasks. The sources are complementary rather than conflicting—the RAG Report evaluates retrieval of labelled text chunks, whereas LegalBench benchmarks discrete interpretation tasks. Material internal variation concerns scope and method: the RAG findings do not establish end-to-end legal analysis and are limited to particular chunking and text formats; LegalBench does not test retrieval optimisation or establish deployment reliability. Neither source demonstrates readiness for unsupervised legal work, explains all causes of score variation, or measures human verification requirements.
